claims.text: The high-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by the synthesis annealing profile.
The initial nanoparticles are kinetically trapped, homogeneous, metastable solid solutions.
Atomic diffusion and aggregation cause phase segregation or precipitate formation.
Short dwell times and rapid cooling limit the time available for atomic diffusion.
Short, rapid annealing maintains high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy and restricted diffusion help preserve a homogeneous solid-solution structure and suppress precipitation.
Prolonged annealing or slow cooling provides enough thermal energy and time for atoms to overcome kinetic barriers.
Overcoming kinetic barriers promotes elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Elemental segregation and secondary phases compromise chemical and structural stability.
Rapidly annealed and quenched nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than nanoparticles subjected to longer dwell times or slower cooling.
Rapidly annealed nanoparticles will sustain greater structural stability during high-temperature service testing.
Long dwell times or slow cooling will produce detectable nanoprecipitates or other signs of segregation.
Segregation induced by long dwell times or slow cooling will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles made by typical synthesis routes without controlled thermal treatment tend to have heterogeneous microstructures.
Nanoparticles made without controlled thermal treatment tend to undergo premature phase separation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The proposed relationship applies within service-temperature ranges where thermally activated diffusion is significant.
Additional stabilization, such as high noble-metal content, can alter the proposed annealing–stability relationship.
Critical dwell times and cooling rates depend on elemental properties such as atomic radii and bonding preferences.
The tested annealing temperatures span 773–1173 K for catalytic applications and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications.
